extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in humour research and joke-writing (journalists, amateur joke-writers, social scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings about what makes short jokes funny to large, diverse audiences (cross-cultural and demographic insights, optimal length, content cues). Useful for joke-writers, popular researchers, and communicators aiming for broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three elements central to humour
rubrics_metrics.description: It also contained the three elements that were found central to humour: a sense of superiority, an unexpected response, and a sad feeling of mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong jokes often combine multiple elements: (1) a sense of superiority (the audience feeling ‘above’ the target), (2) an unexpected response or misdirection that surprises, and (3) a bittersweet or mortality-tinged undertone. Example: the winning 'hunters' joke contains all three. Aim to include at least one of these, and combinations tend to be especially effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural / national preferences for joke types
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughlab established that the British, Irish, New Zealanders and Australians prefer a play on words and that the French, Danes and Belgians have a taste for the surreal. Americans and Canadians, on the other hand, chuckle at jokes showing one group's superiority over another. The Germans apparently have the broadest sense of humour - if only because they have no national preference, and therefore find almost anything funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose joke type to match audience culture: use puns/play-on-words for UK/ANZ audiences; surreal or absurd humour for certain continental audiences; superiority-based jokes tend to work better in North America. Germans may accept many types. Tailor content to national/cultural expectations to increase appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal joke length (~103 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the data, jokes containing 103 are the funniest. Interestingly, the winning 'hunters' joke is 102 words long - almost the perfect length for a joke!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting short-form jokes for broad online/public consumption, aiming for roughly 100–105 words may increase perceived funniness. This is an empirical central tendency from LaughLab data, not a strict rule—brevity and pacing still matter—but word-count can affect rhythm, buildup, and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal references: ducks are funnier
rubrics_metrics.description: The researchers found that jokes mentioning ducks were seen as funnier than other jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If including an animal in a joke, a duck tended to score higher in the dataset. This is a quirky empirical finding (possibly due to shape/behaviour associations); use it as a lightweight heuristic when experimenting with animal-based humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty versus recognition / memory activation
rubrics_metrics.description: With each joke, a specific area at the front of the volunteer's brain lit up. There was also a reaction in an area linked to memory, showing recognition of an old joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour engages frontal brain regions (processing surprise/misdirection) and memory areas (recognition of familiar jokes). Novel misdirection that triggers recognition or recall can enhance response, but mere repetition (recognizable but stale jokes) may not elicit laughter. Balancing novelty with recognizable frames can be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused/cliché formats and repeated submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: One joke - 'What's brown and sticky? A stick' - was submitted 300 times, and nobody ever found it funny. Laughlab also nominated a candidate for worst joke: 'Knock knock.' - 'Who's there?' - 'Boo' - 'Boo who?' - 'Don't cry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overused one-liners, clichéd punchlines, and tired formats (e.g., badly executed knock-knock jokes) score poorly. Novelty and freshness are important; repeated, familiar jokes are unlikely to be rated funny regardless of frequency of submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and situational context affect funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful analysis of the data revealed that people found the jokes funniest on the 7th October at 6.03 in the evening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived funniness can vary with time/date and situational context (time of day, mood of audience). Consider timing and setting when presenting jokes—audience receptiveness fluctuates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and demographic variation in receptiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In a study of British regional variation, the Welsh were the keenest on jokes in general, and the Scots were the least keen. The project produced an exhaustive breakdown of humour by age, sex and nationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience demographic (age, sex, region) affects how humour is received. Test material with target demographic slices and adapt content and delivery to regional tastes and sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority-based humour produces a feel-better effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr Gosall had liked the joke for years. He said: 'It makes people feel better … reminds you that there's always someone out there doing something more stupid than you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes that let audiences feel a sense of superiority (comparing themselves favorably to a bumbling character) can produce cathartic or feel-better laughter. Use this dynamic cautiously—it can be effective but risks offending if directed at vulnerable groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection and punchline timing (example structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The winning joke: setup (friend appears dead), expected help-seeking, operator's instruction 'make sure he's dead', silence, then a shot and the stunned follow-up 'OK, now what?' — an unexpected response leading to a darkly comic payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective joke structure often uses a believable setup, a plausible instruction or cue, a short pause/silence to create tension, and an unexpected action/response as the punchline. Pacing (including well-placed silence) and the surprise/action as payoff are key to maximizing laughter, especially in narrative/dark-humour formats.
